meta.note: The hours are the course's planning ranges (20 to 40 hours for the study, CK-R's four among them), not measurements. The exemplar studies (a co-op feeder, Prairie City's weatherization programme, a co-op's community solar, the Plains Grid in a heat wave) and their numbers are fictional and illustrative: assumed, not computed, except the cost and CO₂ fragment, whose arithmetic the page shows and the test redoes. Method families: the ids of R3's data file (r03-system-and-method.json), whose labels the page reads. Read by assets/learn/cr-your-own-study.js; the page's static blocks are written from this file by node _tests/learn/test_cr-your-own-study.js --write.

tracks.label: Model-based
tracks.builds: A model of the system that answers what to do, or what would happen.
tracks.trust: Reruns from a [[clean-clone|clean clone]]; checked against a hand calculation or a published benchmark, and validated against real data.

tracks.label: Empirical
tracks.short: data analysis, or a reproduction or replication of a published result
tracks.builds: An analysis of observed data; or a published result rerun with its own data and code (a computational reproduction), or tested on new data (a replication).
tracks.trust: Reruns from a clean clone, raw data to result; a reproduction or a replication reports how close it came to the published number.

tracks.label: Mixed
tracks.short: a model or data analysis with a stakeholder or qualitative part
tracks.builds: Numbers and people's reasons, with a plan for how each informs the other.
tracks.trust: A clean-clone rerun for the numbers; an audit trail from raw notes to themes for the qualitative part.

stages.label: Question
stages.does: Turn your question card into one you can answer at your scale, with its boundary.
done: Your card passes its eight checks.
You can say what answer would change your audience's decision.

stages.label: Literature
stages.does: Search open databases, [[snowballing|snowball]] from a review, and map what is known.
done: A [[concept-matrix|concept matrix]] of at least 12 sources.
A gap stated with evidence, from a search a reviewer can repeat.

stages.label: Method
stages.does: Choose a method family, defend it, and write the one-page proposal.
done: The method defended against two alternatives, one from another family.
Milestone: the proposal.

stages.label: Data
stages.does: Get, clean and document your data, or plan and hold your interviews.
done: A data note: each source with its date and licence.
A cleaning log; for interviews, consent forms and a guide.

stages.label: Build and validate
stages.does: Build the model or analysis under version control, verify it, and validate one result.
done: It reruns from a [[clean-clone|clean clone]] (or a complete audit trail).
A verification log.
One validation against real data or an independent reference.

stages.label: Uncertainty and accounting
stages.does: Classify the uncertainties, treat each one, and put cost and carbon on one boundary.
done: Uncertainties classified.
Scenarios or a global sensitivity analysis; results as ranges.
Cost and emissions on one boundary where you report both.

stages.label: Mock review and rerun
stages.does: Get a written mock review of your question and method, answer it, revise, and rerun your main result.
done: Every major concern answered.
A change log.
A clean-clone rerun within your tolerance, or the difference explained.

stages.label: Paper and poster
stages.does: Write the paper and the poster, with each result's limits beside it.
done: A six-page paper with one key figure.
A limits paragraph and a 150-word public summary.
A poster.

stages.label: Integrity and release
stages.does: Check licences, credit and conflicts; treat the people your study is about fairly; release what you may.
done: Licences checked; credit and conflicts stated.
The people the study is about treated fairly.
Data and code released with documentation where allowed.
Your rubric sheet.

uncertainty.label: Scenarios
uncertainty.line: Scenarios for the uncertainties classified as scenario or deep, each result reported per scenario.

uncertainty.label: Global sensitivity analysis
uncertainty.line: A global sensitivity analysis, every uncertain input varied together, results as ranges.

uncertainty.label: Monte Carlo
uncertainty.line: Monte Carlo over the inputs classified as parameter uncertainty, varied together, results as ranges.

uncertainty.label: Stochastic or robust optimization
uncertainty.line: Stochastic or robust optimization over stated scenarios, with the plan's cost in each.

uncertainty.label: Intervals and robustness checks
uncertainty.line: Confidence intervals, and the main estimate rerun under other reasonable specifications.

uncertainty.label: Triangulation
uncertainty.line: Triangulation: each qualitative finding checked against a second source or method.

uncertainty.label: One input at a time
uncertainty.line: One input swung at a time, the others at their base values.
uncertainty.why: Swings one at a time miss interactions; the rubric's Proficient level asks for scenarios or a global sensitivity analysis.

reviews.label: A mentor
reviews.line: A mentor reviews the proposal, the validation evidence and the final study.

reviews.label: A peer (the swap)
reviews.line: A peer and you swap proposals and review each other's with CK-R's form.

reviews.label: Yourself, after a day away
reviews.line: You review your own proposal with CK-R's form, a day after you last edited it.

fields.label: Why it matters
fields.hint: Who would act on the answer, and what answer would change their decision.

fields.label: What is known, and the gap
fields.hint: The three closest studies and what none of them answers; the size of your concept matrix and the date of your search (R2).

fields.label: Why this method, not the alternatives
fields.hint: What your method answers that the two alternatives cannot (name a same-family one exactly), and one limit you will mitigate (R3).

fields.label: Data and licences
fields.hint: Each source, its date and its licence; for interviews, who you will ask and how you will ask for consent (R4, R9).

fields.label: How you will check it
fields.hint: One verification check, one validation against real data or an independent reference, and the tolerance you set now (R5).

fields.label: What the study leaves out
fields.hint: The parts, people and years outside your boundary, and why that does not change the answer to your question.

fields.label: Integrity
fields.hint: Credit, conflicts, consent, and who the study affects (R9).

studies.feeder: A co-op's farm [[feeder|feeder]]: how much battery, and which tariff, keep the summer evening peak under the feeder's limit at least cost (model-based, prescriptive, S1)
studies.weather: Prairie City's 2023 [[weatherization|weatherization]] programme: did weatherized homes use less gas than homes on its waiting list (empirical, evaluative, S3)
studies.solar: A co-op's community solar: why some farms joined and others did not, from sign-up records and 12 interviews (mixed, explanatory, S1)
studies.heat: The Plains Grid in a five-day heat wave: how often the reserve falls short with more air conditioning (model-based, predictive, S2)

exemplars.title: Framing: the question
exemplars.task: Write the study's question as a card.

parts.text: Is weatherization good for Prairie City?
parts.note: No type, no audience, no metric, no comparison: nobody could say when it is answered.

answers.label: Strong

parts.text: use less gas
parts.note: A metric; its units follow.

parts: in the next two winters than

parts.text: similar homes still on the waiting list?
parts.note: The counterfactual: homes that applied too.

parts.text: the city's housing office, which sets next year's budget and would cut the programme if the saving is under 5%.
parts.note: Who acts on the answer, and the answer that would change the decision.

parts:
Metric: winter gas use per home, kWh, adjusted for the weather.
Scale: S3; boundary: the homes' gas, not their electricity.

parts.text: Wrong if: the waiting-list homes' use fell as much.
parts.note: A falsification statement.

exemplars.title: Positioning: the gap
exemplars.task: State what is known and the gap.

parts.text: few studies look at weatherization in Prairie City, so this study is novel.
parts.note: Few studies is not evidence of a gap, or of novelty: the topic may be unimportant, or the search poor.

parts.text: of the 14 studies in my concept matrix, 9 use billing data and 3 compare with a waiting list;
parts.note: The map behind the claim: a matrix of more than 12 sources.

parts.text: none of the 3 is in a city with winters this cold.
parts.note: The empty cell, stated precisely.

parts.text: OpenAlex, with the string and the date in appendix A; two more studies found, both in milder climates.
parts.note: A dated search a reviewer can repeat.

parts.text: a waiting-list study in a milder city; this one adds cold winters and a second winter.
parts.note: The closest prior work, engaged directly.

exemplars.title: Method fit: the choice
exemplars.task: Choose the method and defend it.

parts.text: optimization, because I used it in M2.
parts.note: Chosen by habit.

parts.text: a linear program of the feeder's summer evenings: the question asks what to do, under stated rules.
parts.note: The family fits the question's type (prescriptive); a [[linear-program|linear program]] is one kind of optimization.

parts.text: it tests the designs it is given, but does not search for the cheapest.
parts.note: One alternative, and why not.

parts.text: it would capture how members respond, but needs behaviour data the co-op does not have.
parts.note: A second alternative, from another family.

parts.text: perfect foresight flatters the battery; I rerun with a day-ahead forecast.
parts.note: A limit of the chosen method, stated and partly mitigated ([[perfect-foresight|perfect foresight]]).

exemplars.title: Trustworthy analysis: the log
exemplars.task: Write an entry of the verification log.

parts.text: checked the model; results look reasonable.
parts.note: No check named, no reference, no tolerance: nobody can repeat it.

parts.text: holds in every hour (largest error 0.000 kW).
parts.note: A verification check, named, with its result.

parts.text: with no battery, the bill equals the hand calculation to the cent.
parts.note: An independent reference, worked by hand.

parts.text: the feeder's metered 2025 evening peak, 2.81 MW, against the model's 2.76 MW: 1.8% low, inside the 5% set beforehand.
parts.note: Real data, with a tolerance set before looking.

parts.text: from a clean clone, the same result.
parts.note: Reproducible from the repository alone ([[clean-clone|clean clone]]). Strong would add a rerun by someone else.

parts.text: the reserve falls short in 4 hours of the heat wave.
parts.note: A single number, as if certain.

parts.text: in 90% of 1,000 Monte Carlo runs the reserve falls short in 1 to 9 hours of the heat wave, against 0 to 2 hours with today's air conditioning.
parts.note: A range, how it was made, and what it is compared with.

parts.text: air-conditioning growth moves it most, then the gas fleet's outage rate.
parts.note: The uncertainties that matter, ranked. Strong would add what knowing them better is worth to the decision.

parts.text: we treat a heat wave hotter than any on record as a stress scenario, because we cannot defend a probability for it.
parts.note: [[deep-uncertainty|Deep uncertainty]] kept out of the probabilities: the evidence, not the record alone, decides it.

parts.text: the battery saves money and cuts emissions a lot.
parts.note: Whose money, on what boundary, against what?

parts.text: against no battery, the co-op's power bill falls $250,000 a year; less the battery's annualized cost, $160,000, its yearly cost falls $90,000 (2025 dollars).
parts.note: Whose money, against what, in which dollars: the bill's fall less the battery's yearly cost.

parts.text: 120 t a year less, location-based with the grid's hourly average factors, on the same boundary: the co-op's purchases.
parts.note: One boundary for cost and carbon; the emissions question named ([[location-based|location-based]]).

parts.text: it buys 2,000 MWh at night (0.39 t CO₂ per MWh) to deliver 1,800 MWh in the evening (0.50 t per MWh): 1,800 × 0.50 − 2,000 × 0.39 = 900 − 780 = 120 t.
parts.note: The arithmetic, its 10% losses included. With one yearly factor for every hour, the 200 MWh lost would add CO₂ instead.

parts.text: members pay for the battery through rates; farms on the feeder gain most.
parts.note: Who pays and who benefits, named.

exemplars.title: Realism: the inputs
exemplars.task: Say what the key inputs are, and what the study leaves out.

parts.text: the co-op's new 2 MW battery is installed in 2027.
parts.note: An option written as if it were a project that exists.

parts.text: a design option; the co-op has decided nothing.
parts.note: Evidence status: an option, not an announced or built project.

parts.text: the co-op's published 2025 tariff, dated.
parts.note: A primary document for a key input.

parts.text: the feeder's voltage limits, battery wear after year 10, and how members respond to the tariff.
parts.note: A list of what the analysis leaves out.

exemplars.title: Communication: the public summary
exemplars.task: Write the core of the 150-word public summary.

parts.text: our study proves weatherization works and should be extended to every home.
parts.note: Proves, works, every home: no size, no limits, and a policy the study did not test.

parts.text: weatherized homes used 9% to 15% less gas in the two winters after than similar homes still on the waiting list.
parts.note: The finding, with its size and its comparison.

parts.text: one city, two winters, homes that applied; gas use, not comfort or health.
parts.note: The limits beside the result.

parts.text: the result holds for homes like those that applied; homes that never apply may differ.
parts.note: A reading that is hard to misread.

parts.text: no issues: the data are public.
parts.note: The interviews and the co-op's records are not public: consent and licences unchecked.

parts.text: the 12 interviewees signed a consent form, and the university's ethics board approved the interviews.
parts.note: [[informed-consent|Consent]] and [[ethics-board|ethics review]] for the people the study is about.

parts.text: the co-op's sign-up records under a data-sharing agreement, names removed; I release the code and a synthetic copy, not the records.
parts.note: The licence checked; released where allowed ([[synthetic-sample|a synthetic copy]]).

parts.text: co-op staff in the acknowledgements; no funding and no conflicts.
parts.note: Credit and conflicts stated.

parts.text: the co-op saw them before publication, with no veto.
parts.note: Stakeholders treated fairly, without control of the results.

rubric.look: Your proposal's question card passes its eight checks and says what answer would change your audience's decision.
Your concept matrix of 12 sources or more, and a dated search behind the gap.
Your method defended against the two alternatives in your plan, and one limit you mitigated.
A clean-clone rerun (CK-R), a verification log and one validation, named in the paper.
The main result as a range, with how the range was made.
Cost and emissions on one boundary where you report them, the emissions question named, and who pays and who benefits.
The evidence status of your key inputs, and a list of what the study leaves out.
The six-page paper, its key figure, the limits paragraph and the 150-word public summary.
Your integrity statement: licences, credit, conflicts and consent; what you released.

statuses.requires: The core path, the checkpoints CK-F, CK-A and CK-M, and a submitted CR with a self-assessment.
statuses.evidence: The CR repository and report, the rubric sheet.

statuses.status: Demonstrated supervised-project readiness at scale Sx
statuses.requires: The above, plus the Sx route, CK-R, and Proficient or better on all nine rubric competences. A mentor's review of the proposal, the validation evidence and the final study is optional but recommended.
statuses.evidence: The same, plus the CK-R review and response, and the mentor's comments if any.
